Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia

What could be worse for the president than the criticisms is that the announced ceasefire has had little effect on the price of diesel, which continues to sit below its record highs but still well above $6 a gallon.

Meanwhile, as the latest twists in the Russia-Ukraine conflict unfolded, new violence in the Middle East threaten to further strain global energy markets, regardless of what happens with Russian oil.

A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia , including strikes on airports and energy infrastructure that killed at least 13 over the weekend, have threatened to escalate a decade-long conflict that had been simmering throughout the US-Iran war.

"This is the Houthis sending a message that it's not just military targets, it's not just energy infrastructure, they're going to strike at civilian airports that could kill a lot of people," Michael Ratney, former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told the BBC.

The US-Iran war was a conflict that none of the Arab nations in the region wanted, he said, and the latest Houthi offensive was a foreseeable result. With the US and Iran currently in an extended stand-off, any new hostilities could lead to more regional conflict and send oil prices soaring once more.

"I do think it gets uglier before it really deescalates," he said.

In recent weeks, Trump has pointed to Ukraine, not the Middle East, as the primary source of the world's energy woes. He cites increased oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which had been effectively shut by Iran's military threat.

That may, however, be wishful thinking – an attempt to convince the American public to direct their energy-related anger toward a conflict that began under a different president's watch.

There is only one president at a time, however. And when American voters casts their ballots they tend to hold those who are currently in power responsible.

After a rough weekend that again proved there are no easy fixes to the global energy crisis, that may be the worst news of all for the US president.

articles.title: Trump’s antitrust threat to NBC, CBS, ABC, CNN and Fox News: What to know
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) took many by surprise when it said over the weekend it would investigate the country’s top television networks on antitrust grounds over a boycott the TV networks carried out last month in response to President Trump’s ban of three news outlets from the White House. The announcement came as…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) took many by surprise when it said over the weekend it would investigate the country’s top television networks on antitrust grounds over a boycott the TV networks carried out last month in response to President Trump’s ban of three news outlets from the White House.

The announcement came as a federal judge is weighing the legality of an effort by the West Wing to keep CNN, one of the networks targeted by Trump’s ban, from carrying out its duties in the press pool rotation.

The pool is a rotating group of reporters that travels with and covers the president. The television pool includes a broadcast shared among the networks.

The episode is being seen as a major escalation in Trump’s ongoing war with the national press corps and underscores his continued effort to push back on independent reporting of news organizations.

Here’s what to know about the Trump administration’s latest salvo against the media.

The DOJ is probing whether the five major TV networks — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — had violated federal antitrust law by boycotting their duties working together to pool coverage of the president.

The five networks briefly stopped providing pool coverage of Trump’s daily activities after he included one of its member outlets, CNN, in a ban of three news organizations from White House grounds.

Despite a federal judge ordering the ban lifted two weeks later, the White House has continued to keep CNN from carrying out pool duties.

The boycott by the major TV networks was seen as an act of solidarity with CNN. The networks said in a joint statement at the time that “no administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

Trump’s DOJ argues it could be a violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act, a law passed more than 100 years ago designed to stop monopolies in major American businesses and protect competition.

A DOJ spokesperson in a statement called the decision to hold back pool coverage a “group boycott among commercial competitors” and said the department was “simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”

Pooling audio and video footage of the president is a long-standing practice in the national media, adhered to in part as a cost saving measure that allows for networks to take turns traveling with the president and disseminating their coverage to dozens of other media outlets, including local stations and smaller publications.

Probe fuels tension between West Wing, journalists

Tensions between the West Wing and media covering the White House have been festering for weeks.

Trump administration officials have argued journalists do not have a First Amendment right to access certain White House spaces such as the Oval Office and Air Force One.

It’s a theory that underpins the West Wing’s efforts against CNN and was also used to punish The Associated Press last year over the wire service’s refusal to refer to the body of water south of the United States as the “Gulf of America.”

After a federal judge issued an order temporarily lifting the White House’s ban on the three outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — pool coverage by the networks resumed.

There have been two exceptions so far: both when it was CNN’s turn to travel with the president and journalists from the outlet were blocked from doing so by West Wing staff.

The president has accused each of the networks of publishing “fake news” about his administration — news that he argues endangers national security.

Trump has called out reporters from the outlets by name and said repeatedly that he has a “right” to “clear out the fake news,” despite the judge’s ruling.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, is slated to rule on the First Amendment issue related to pool coverage specifically this week.

Press freedom, antitrust experts slam DOJ probe

A growing number of experts on antitrust law and press freedom advocates are casting doubt on the veracity of the DOJ’s move to probe the networks over their temporary boycott.

Bringing an antitrust case against media outlets protected by the First Amendment could be on shaky legal ground, these voices say.

“They would have to show the collective action of these networks is being done for a commercial advantage, and I just don’t see it here,” William Kovacic, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), told The Hill on Monday.

Holding back pool coverage of the president, Kovacic said, came out of “genuine concern about the coverage of the news. And that’s right in the center of the First Amendment bullseye.”

“It’s not like they’re trying to get better advertising rates or more subscribers or achieve measurable economic advantage,” the former FTC chair added. “I see it as truly an expression of opposition to an effort by the government to control the news.”

Others suggested it is unlikely the DOJ takes any action against the networks in court.

“Harming Trump’s ego or his craving for attention is not a competitive harm redressable through antitrust law,” said Seth Stern, head of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation. “I don’t know whether they care so much if they lose in court. They’re throwing spaghetti at the wall and hoping something sticks.”

Judge set to rule on First Amendment protections for TV poolers

Kelly’s temporary injunction lifting the ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico is set to expire Tuesday, meaning the Trump administration could feasibly keep the outlets from the White House grounds again if the judge takes no further action.

The judge initially ruled the government had violated the due process rights of the three outlets and seemed skeptical of the Trump administration’s argument that media companies had endangered national security.

Trump has attacked Kelly in the past, calling him “totally disloyal” and saying the judge would “probably” rule against him. The DOJ is expected to appeal any ruling Kelly makes on the First Amendment issue relating to press access.

Some observers say the DOJ’s probe is a sign the boycott responding to the ban got under the president’s skin and feeds into a political game Trump has been playing against the media for years.

“Trump has spent all this time telling everyone how much he hates the press and wishes they would go away, so you think he would say good riddance if they decided not to cover him,” said Stern, the press freedom attorney. “But apparently that spooked him that the news outlets were able to shut off his megaphone for a few days. It looks like he ended up missing the press more than he thought he would.”

articles.title: Trump says he ‘never thought’ he’d have to hold rallies again
articles.summary: President Trump said Sunday he “never thought” he would hold rallies again as he crisscrosses the country to campaign for Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections. Trump made the observation while letting Truth Social followers know he would campaign for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy in Youngstown, Ohio, on…
articles.body:
President Trump said Sunday he “never thought” he would hold rallies again as he crisscrosses the country to campaign for Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections.

Trump made the observation while letting Truth Social followers know he would campaign for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy in Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday. On Tuesday, we will join Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and Rep. Nick Begich (R-Alaska) for a rally in Wasilla, Alaska.

“My Rallies, legendary they have already become, have made a tremendous difference with the enthusiasm of the Republican Party,” he wrote on Truth Social. “They have been waiting for them to happen, even though I never thought I’d have to be doing Rallies again.”

“The good news is, I love them, the music, and the incredible enthusiasm, and will always be in favor of what’s good for America — and that means the Republican Party,” Trump added.

Trump is continuing his red-state campaign swing with stops in Montana and Georgia slated for later this week. The tour through traditionally red states has raised some eyebrows, however. A Republican source told The Hill earlier this month the trips are part of a strategy to replicate his presidential turnout for the midterms, comparing it to “hitting two birds with one stone.”

Trump’s rallies have been a signature point of both his administrations and all three of his campaigns for president. The rallies have given him a pulpit to explain his agenda, insult political opponents and critics, crack jokes and quip at protesters who disrupt his rallies.

NBC News reported before Trump’s 2024 election win that until that point, the president had held 900 rallies since June 2015, when he launched his first presidential campaign. He has held dozens of rallies going into the 2026 midterms, with eight rallies held so far in October, the outlet reported .

The president has urged Republican voters to “pretend” that he’s on the ballot , separately warning GOP lawmakers that Democrats will impeach him if they reclaim control of Congress. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has echoed this warning , saying that it’s “guaranteed, probably on the first day.”

“Remember, they’ve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress,” Johnson told Scott Jennings, a pro-Trump pundit, in an interview last Tuesday. “And they’re raring to go.”

The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ estimated Monday that Democrats hold a 76 percent probability of winning back the House, while the party has a narrower fight to reclaim the Senate with a 56 percent probability .

articles.title: Christie: GOP committing ‘malpractice’ to try to win Congress
articles.summary: Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) said Sunday the GOP is committing “malpractice” in its efforts to retain control of Congress amid a tough midterm environment for the party. Christie — a former Republican presidential candidate — discussed the surprisingly competitive Senate election in Kansas while appearing on ABC News’s “This Week.” “As a…
articles.body:
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) said Sunday the GOP is committing “malpractice” in its efforts to retain control of Congress amid a tough midterm environment for the party.

Christie — a former Republican presidential candidate — discussed the surprisingly competitive Senate election in Kansas while appearing on ABC News’s “ This Week .”

“As a Republican, I sat here shaking my head at the political malpractice that was committed on this air with you [host Jonathan Karl] by [House Majority Whip] Tom Emmer [(R-Minn.)],” he said.

Christie said he identified three cornerstones to “the Republican argument for the last three weeks.” He first drew attention to President Trump’s controversial oil deal , which Christie argued will give Russia the money “to kill free Ukrainians.”

The former governor also pointed to rising prices “at the grocery store and at the gas station” which he said the GOP is trying to avoid and reframe as “American people don’t get the fact that the economy is great.”

Christie then mentioned the Pentagon’s recent decision to livestream the execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan.

“This is malpractice, and the fact is Tom is smarter than that. He knows better than that. But what you heard throughout it is this absolute requirement that you must stand by everything Donald Trump says and does,” Christie continued.

“If you want to remain in leadership in the House or the Senate, and it is, it is malpractice to good Republicans all across this country who care about the issues we care about,” he said.

Christie ran for president in 2016 before becoming a Trump ally during the president’s first term. That changed when he ran against Trump in the Republican primaries in 2024. In September, he teased a third potential presidential bid but said it would depend on the 2026 midterm results.

The upcoming election has Democrats favored to win the House and, more narrowly, the Senate this fall, according to the latest forecasts from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, amid problematic approval numbers for the president and growing voter anger over the economy under a Republican-led Washington.

Kansas’s Senate race seems to be emblematic of this pattern as incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) struggles against Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton. DDHQ also wrote in a polling analysis that Hamilton gives Democrats an “outside shot” of flipping Kansas’s Senate seat.

articles.title: Bessent on how Iran war ends: ‘I don’t know’
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday he was unsure how the Iran war will end, with the eight-month mark of the conflict nearing. “I don’t know what ‘crying uncle’ is in Farsi, but they’re going to be crying uncle. You know, they are collapsing. They can’t pay their soldiers. And Rachel, I don’t know how…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday he was unsure how the Iran war will end, with the eight-month mark of the conflict nearing.

“I don’t know what ‘crying uncle’ is in Farsi, but they’re going to be crying uncle. You know, they are collapsing. They can’t pay their soldiers. And Rachel, I don’t know how this ends. You never know how this ends,” Bessent told Fox News’s Rachel Campos-Duffy on “Fox & Friends Weekend,” talking about Iran.

“That — the Berlin Wall just came down one day. We don’t know whether the people rise up, the IRGC turn on each other, or they actually come to their senses and want to make a deal not to have a nuclear program,” he added, referring to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.

Bessent’s comments come about two weeks before the war with Iran hits the eight-month mark. The war, which is broadly unpopular with the American public, has driven up energy costs in the U.S. as the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil exports from the Persian Gulf, has been closed amid the conflict.

The war and its downstream effects have also become a central issue in this year’s midterms, with Democrats hammering Republicans over the conflict and the higher energy costs it has brought.

Trump initially predicted the war would last for a few weeks, but has struggled to find an off-ramp despite the political pain at home. He has recently said it will end soon after the midterms, but has remained vague on how that will happen.

Last week, he said the U.S. would not launch new strikes against Iran before the midterms. The prolonged war has spurred mounting concerns about diminished U.S. weapons stockpiles and the steep cost to friendly countries in the region.

On Friday, the Defense Department updated the number of American service members dead in the Iran war to 21.

The two deaths, which did not happen in combat, recently added to the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System were Army Maj. Sorffly Davius and an unidentified Navy sailor, a U.S. official told The Hill over the weekend.

articles.summary: President Trump confirmed reports that he is considering firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, amid misconduct allegations. “Well, we’re looking at it. Yeah, we’re not happy,” Trump told The Hill when speaking with reporters Monday on the White House South Lawn. The Wall Street Journal first reported last week that Guilfoyle asked Trump…
articles.body:
President Trump confirmed reports that he is considering firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, amid misconduct allegations.

“Well, we’re looking at it. Yeah, we’re not happy,” Trump told The Hill when speaking with reporters Monday on the White House South Lawn.

The Wall Street Journal first reported last week that Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay a $100,000 credit card bill and instructed him to do so via wire transfer to avoid a paper trail.

The Associated Press then reported Sunday that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were considering firing Guilfoyle, who serves as the U.S. ambassador to Greece.

Over the weekend, the Journal also reported that senior Trump administration officials were discussing the ambassador’s future in her post and that a decision from Trump would be coming shortly. The news outlet reported new allegations that wealthy Greek businessmen helped fund Guilfoyle’s luxury travel as she used her role to promote their business interests too.

The allegations against Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to Donald Trump Jr., have sparked backlash from both sides of the aisle.

Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) called the reports “troubling” during an interview with CBS News’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday.

“Well, what we’ve seen in the reports is very troubling. It’s concerning. And I’m sure there’s going to be an investigation. I would assume the State Department would be conducting that,” Barrasso said.

“I know that the Senate Foreign Relations Committee will have oversight and look into that as well. But I think the public has a right to know what was — what is found, and it is quite a bit of concern,” he continued.

articles.title: Trump calls Omar ‘totally crooked’ in first remarks on raid
articles.summary: President Trump called Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) “totally crooked” in his first remarks since federal agents searched her home as part of ongoing criminal investigations. “Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” he told reporters before departing the White House for Ohio. “I’ve always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that…
articles.body:
President Trump called Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) “totally crooked” in his first remarks since federal agents searched her home as part of ongoing criminal investigations.

“Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” he told reporters before departing the White House for Ohio. “I’ve always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me.”

“I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ [Department of Justice],” he continued. “I have nothing to do with it.”

Agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) — the investigative arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) — carried out the search of the Somali-born lawmaker’s Washington, D.C. home Monday.

“This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” the DOJ said in its statement.

A source familiar with the investigation told Reuters that the probe is related to alleged immigration fraud and concerns part of her immigration papers that were filled out by her father when she was a child. She got her citizenship in 2000.

Omar on social media condemned the raid, calling it “political intimidation.”

“I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” she wrote on social media Monday. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

The raid comes roughly a month after White House border czar Tom Homan said there was a federal criminal investigation involving Omar.

“If someone committed an immigration violation, if someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law. So, I’ll leave it at that. We’ll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations, continue the investigation,” Homan said during an appearance on Fox News.

Trump and other Republicans have repeatedly targeted Omar, a vocal critic of the administration and part of the “squad” of progressive House members in Congress. The president has repeatedly bashed Somalia and Somali Americans in Minnesota.

“The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week. “The people of Minnesota must fight back.”

After Trump called Omar “garbage” earlier this year, she said: “His obsession with me is creepy. I hope he gets the help he desperately needs.”

articles.body:
President Trump says that Russia and Ukraine had reached an energy ceasefire after he said Russia would supply diesel to the global marketplace.

© Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Sunday morning. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”

The president previously announced an energy ceasefire between both countries in mid-September. He wrote on Truth Social at the time that both countries agreed to not hit the other country’s energy infrastructure.

Trump announced this latest energy ceasefire deal after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, in an interview with ABC News’s “This Week,” called for an energy ceasefire from both sides.

“It’s fair deal. It’s not the best deal,” Zelesnky said. “The best deal not –– not to have a war to stop Putin. But the first step is ceasefire, energy ceasefire. OK, if they want energy ceasefire, we are open for this. Don’t attack us. Don’t kill our children. We will stop attack your diesel. And I think it’s fair, fair deal.”

Reports indicated that after the announcement, Russia struck a Ukrainian power plant.

On Monday, Zelensky told Fox News he supported a ceasefire, but said he wasn’t sure if Russian President Vladimir Putin was ready.

articles.title: Trump says ‘we’re looking at’ firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece
articles.summary: The president’s remarks come days after a Trump donor alleged Guilfoyle tried to get him to pay $100,000 to get rid of her credit card debt shortly before her confirmation hearing.
articles.body: President Donald Trump indicated Monday that he’s considering firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former top Trump campaign surrogate who has served as the U.S. ambassador to Greece since 2025. “We’re looking at it,” Trump said when asked if he’s weighing firing Guilfoyle, as first reported by The Associated Press, amid allegations of misconduct related to her role as ambassador. “We’re not happy,” Trump added. His comments come days after he struck a softer tone when asked Friday about her alleged conduct. “I just heard a little bit about it. I don’t know too much, but she was always very nice,” he said at the time. An attorney for Guilfoyle — a former Fox News personality who used to be engaged to Trump’s oldest son, Donald Trump Jr. — did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s remarks Monday. Guilfoyle and the U.S. Embassy in Greece are under investigation by the State Department’s Office of the Inspector General, two people familiar with the decision confirmed to NBC News last week. The probe came after reports in The Wall Street Journal of misconduct in her role as ambassador, including allegedly bragging about her connections to Greek tycoons who she said funded luxury trips for her. The story cited people who heard the conversation and an audio recording. The reports have not been independently confirmed by NBC News. Last week, a Trump donor named Eric Deters came forward accusing Guilfoyle of asking him to pay her outstanding $100,000 American Express bill in the days before her 2025 confirmation hearing in the Senate in exchange for access to senior administration officials. “She was so desperate for that $100,000. It was a quid pro quo,” Deters told NBC News in an interview last week. “She said I could ask her for anything and everything in Trump world. There was no request too big,” he said, adding he did not pay her the money. Attorneys for Guilfoyle have not responded to requests for comment from NBC News about the allegations, but told The Associated Press that Deters had owed her the money for speaking engagements, which he denies. The attorneys, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also denied allegations of any impropriety involving her travel, telling AP in a statement that she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations.”

articles.title: Montana Democratic Party chair resigns, endorses independent in Senate race
articles.summary: Shannon O’Brien, chair of the Montana Democratic Party, on Monday announced her resignation and endorsed Montana independent Senate candidate Seth Bodnar weeks ahead of the November midterm elections. O’Brien, who had served as the state party chair since 2025, wrote in an op-ed on MS NOW that “the Montana Democratic Party is more divided than…
articles.body:
Shannon O’Brien, chair of the Montana Democratic Party, on Monday announced her resignation and endorsed Montana independent Senate candidate Seth Bodnar weeks ahead of the November midterm elections.

O’Brien, who had served as the state party chair since 2025, wrote in an op-ed on MS NOW that “the Montana Democratic Party is more divided than ever” because of the Senate race. She slammed Republican Senate candidate Kurt Alme as someone who “will be a puppet” for President Trump.

Of Senate Democratic candidate Alani Bankhead, O’Brien wrote that there are “real questions” about her “commitment to protecting a woman’s right to choose, her support of working people and her views of people living in poverty.”

“I’m a person with a positive outlook,” O’Brien wrote. “I’m uncomfortable being negative about anyone, especially a Democratic nominee. But sometimes it’s impossible to stay quiet; sometimes you have to make people uncomfortable for the greater good. The winner of this race will almost certainly vote on a nominee to the Supreme Court.”

She accused Bankhead of not having the resources “or will” to win the Senate race, and argued that she “came out of the gate mudslinging at Bodnar, a decent human being, seemingly ignoring the Republican and her ideological opposite.”

“Democrats should ask themselves why Republicans so badly wanted her on the ballot,” she wrote.

The Hill has reached out to Bankhead’s campaign for comment.

O’Brien closed her op-ed writing that Bodnar built his campaign on fixing a Washington that “stopped working for [Montanans] a while ago.”

“Our solutions must be bold, and sometimes uncomfortable, steps toward positive change,” she wrote. “The future of our state and our country is at stake. I hope all Democrats across Montana will join me in choosing the best person this year, even if he’s not from the party they were expecting.”

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s election partner, finds that Alme has a 91 percent probability of winning the Senate race, with Bodnar holding a 9 percent probability.

If the race were held Monday, DDHQ’s aggregate polling suggests that 43.4 percent of Montana voters say they would back Alme, followed by 27.1 percent who would vote for Bodnar and 18.3 percent who say they would support Bankhead.

The race has remained somewhat competitive, with all three candidates and Libertarian Kyle Austin competing for retiring Sen. Steve Daines’s (R-Mont.) open Senate seat. Early polling showed Bodnar could beat Alme in a one-on-one race, but Bankhead has repeatedly said she would not drop out of the race to assist Bodnar’s chances.

“I’ll never bow down … I am in this race to win it, and I am staying through Nov. 3,” she said in August.

articles.title: Trump administration scandals suck up oxygen as Dems seek midterm advantage
articles.summary: Scandals rocking President Trump’s orbit are taking center stage ahead of the midterms as Democrats look for fresh ways to tie their Republican opponents to the president. Last week, a report surfaced indicating Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, privately solicited cash to pay down her debts ahead of her confirmation hearing. Meanwhile, separate reporting…
articles.body:
Scandals rocking President Trump’s orbit are taking center stage ahead of the midterms as Democrats look for fresh ways to tie their Republican opponents to the president.

Last week, a report surfaced indicating Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, privately solicited cash to pay down her debts ahead of her confirmation hearing.

Meanwhile, separate reporting noted Trump’s longtime campaign advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair traveled to the Balkans to advise a pro-Russian political party and made hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Trump told reporters on Monday that he is “looking at” firing Guilfoyle and that he was not happy with her. Last week, he addressed the fallout surrounding Blair and LaCivita’s travel, saying in a TruthSocial post that he would terminate the two if there were any wrongdoing.

Still, Democrats say the reports have aided them in painting Republicans as out of touch in an election hinged on affordability.

“Voters understand that it’s not just that the cost of living has gone up dramatically for them. They understand that it’s gone up dramatically for them and that the administration is prioritizing tax breaks for the wealthy and building ballrooms and building arches and getting rich off of crypto,” said Matt Corridoni, a Democratic operative working with the groups Majority Democrats and The Bench.

Democrats have cited a number of conflict of interest allegations against Trump and those in his orbit.

Ties to his family’s cryptocurrency firm, World Liberty Financial, which he and his sons founded in the fall of 2024 when he was running for president, have drawn particular scrutiny. Financial disclosures show Trump raked in over $500 million from the venture, although the firm has said it has been set up to prevent the Trump family from being involved in the bank while Trump is in the White House.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll released last month found that 69 percent of all adults surveyed said they believed Trump’s businesses influence his decisions as president, including 48 percent of Republicans. Further, 63 percent of respondents said it was inappropriate for Trump and his family to have profited from cryptocurrency.

The president’s critics have also accused the White House ballroom of being a pay-to-play scheme. Trump has received criticism for accepting the Qatari gifted VC-25B Bridge, which is being used as the interim Air Force One, since the deal was announced earlier this term.

Democrats have also used Trump’s ties to the late disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein to paint their Republican opponents in a negative light.

“The corruption story and the abandonment of working people is sort of the central argument that Democrats are making,” said Simon Rosenberg, a Democratic strategist.

“And so every time that there is something that confirms that, it hurts Republicans because it just reinforces one of the central stories that Democrats are telling about the Republican Party,” he continued. “Any additional confirmation of that that’s coming in the national news weakens and hurts the Republicans on the ground.”

Democrats have broadly used the claims against Trump and those around him to paint a picture of a corrupt, Republican-run Washington that is out of touch with the concerns of voters.

“People also are not stupid,” said one Democratic strategist. “When they’re struggling, they’re looking at who is gaining, right?”

“That’s when you sort of peel back the layers and say, ‘Oh it’s these people in office who are benefitting themselves or who are using different things within their power to pass laws to make things easier for them,’” the strategist continued.

The issues took true center stage at midterm debates across the country last week, with Democratic candidates seeking to put their Republican opponents on the defensive.

“The reality is we have a corruption crisis in this country and it is leading to an affordability crisis,” said Iowa Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek, accusing his Republican opponent, Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), and others of using their positions to become wealthier.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) responded to the allegations against Guilfoyle, telling MS NOW that Democratic majorities in Congress were needed to conduct investigations into the matter.

“I think you can rest assured that there will be a focus on congressional oversight, provided we do everything we need to do and regain the majorities necessary to hold this administration accountable,” Ossoff, who is running for reelection in Georgia, told the network.

“We need to plan vigorous oversight efforts, but right now, we need to be relentlessly focused on the imperative of victory,” he continued.

Over the course of his reelection campaign, Ossoff has hammered Trump directly over corruption. Ossoff accused his opponent, Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), of “robbing your constituents to subsidize your donors” during their debate last week.

Corridoni noted a similar issue came up while he was on the campaign trail with Montana Democratic congressional candidate Sam Forstagover the weekend.

“People were bringing up corruption as it relates to cost of living issues,” Corridoni recounted. “The bipartisan audience there was bringing up cuts to health care, the cost of gas, and that they knew this was happening to them while politicians were benefitting from it.”

Republicans have hit back at Democrats, arguing their party has its own corruption issues to tackle.

“Democrats love to lecture voters on corruption, but they have no issue taking millions of dollars from shady billionaires and opposing a congressional stock trading ban to pad their own pockets,” said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary at the Republican National Committee.

“Republicans are the only party that has cut taxes, put workers first, and created thousands of American jobs. Democrats will reverse all these achievements on day one and then get mad when prices rise and more jobs disappear,” she continued.

Rosenberg predicted the battle over corruption would become “a central legislative and oversight fight” if Democrats regain majorities on Capitol Hill.

“They’re [Democrats] are going to have to pass and change the system based on how they’ve campaigned,” he said.

articles.title: The Memo: Trump critics allege abuse of power as Ilhan Omar’s home is raided
articles.summary: Federal agents raided the Washington area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) on Monday, sparking an instant political firestorm. Critics of President Trump immediately cast the raid as an abuse of power victimizing a congresswoman who has been a vigorous opponent of the White House, while conservatives celebrated. The Democratic House leadership released a joint…
articles.body:
Federal agents raided the Washington area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) on Monday, sparking an instant political firestorm.

Critics of President Trump immediately cast the raid as an abuse of power victimizing a congresswoman who has been a vigorous opponent of the White House, while conservatives celebrated.

The Democratic House leadership released a joint statement condemning the raid as “deeply disturbing.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (Mass.) and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar (Calif.) added that the raid “raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries.”

The raid was likened to fascism and called an “unprecedented abuse of power ” by, respectively, Reps. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), both of whom entered Congress along with Omar at the 2018 elections.

Trump, for his part, yet again lambasted Omar in remarks to reporters as he left the White House late on Monday afternoon.

The president called Omar “totally crooked”, without evidence, and derided her as “a terrible person,” but insisted that he had “nothing to do with” the raid.

At a minimum, the raid was an extraordinary moment, with footage of agents carting away boxes from the home of a nationally-known congresswoman less than a month before she seeks reelection.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has typically avoiding such actions during a 60-day window preceding elections, though that practice is a custom rather than a law.

Trump has made a habit of bulldozing his way though such norms, however.

He has been especially avid in doing so in pursuit of his political enemies — as when he sent then-Attorney General Pam Bondi a public message urging her to expedite prosecutions of figures including former FBI Director James Comey; and when he called for the prosecution of six Democratic lawmakers (whom he called “traitors”) who had released a video urging members of the military not to obey illegal orders.

Those efforts have not, by and large, met with ultimate success. The case against Comey has moved slowly, with the former FBI head vigorously protesting his innocence, and a grand jury declined to indict the six Democrats over the video.

But such actions cause serious aggravation, at the very least, for those who find themselves in Trump’s crosshairs.

Omar insisted she was unbowed in a statement posted on social media Monday.

Beginning “I’m OK,” Omar went on to characterize the raid as part of a longer pattern in which, she said, “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns.”

Omar’s post concluded: “I will not be silenced.”

But some of the responses illustrated just how sharply opinion about the Minnesota congresswoman divides along left-right lines.

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), a highly provocative figure in her own right, quote-tweeted Omar’s message and added: “Can she ‘not be silenced’ from Somalia?”

A number of conservative accounts also referenced, or posted a screenshot from a years-old tweet by Omar asserting “No one is above the law.” The tweet dates to Trump’s first impeachment proceedings in 2019.

The polarized debate over the raid on Omar’s home is taking place with very little solid information about what exactly is being investigated, or what evidence is being sought. The DOJ told several news organizations merely that the raid was “part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.”

The Hill noted earlier on Monday that the raid came almost a month after Trump’s border czar Tom Homan had confirmed Omar was being investigated, and implied the probe was centered on allegations of immigration fraud.

Omar, who was born in Somalia in 1982, came to the United States with her family in the mid-1990s. She became a citizen in 2000 and, 16 years later, was elected to the Minnesota statehouse. She was elected to the House two years later.

She has long faced insinuations from conservatives that she abused the immigration process — something that she vigorously denies. Trump and Vice President Vance, among others, have also fueled those accusations.

Omar usually declines to go into detail about those matters — an approach she casts as an appropriate response to allegations she considers lurid and absurd, and which critics cite as evidence she has something to hide.

The New York Times on Monday reported that the most recent investigations into Omar have been “focusing in part on whether her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, lied or omitted information as he sought legal status in the United States before becoming a U.S. citizen.”

If that is true, it would mean the administration was targeting a high-profile political foe for actions her father may or may not have taken roughly 30 years ago.

On the other hand, the Times has also noted that the DOJ during the Biden administration had opened an investigation into Omar “to scrutinize her finances” — though the news organization reported that probe “appears to have stalled for lack of evidence.”

The cloudiness of the picture is not dulling the anger of Trump critics about what took place on Monday, however.

Democratic strategist James Carville told this column that “it’s pretty clear they were targeting her” but added that he would “love to see what was in the affidavit” that earned court approval for the raid.

“Am I highly suspicious it was made up? Yeah, I am,” Carville said, though he added it was important “to find out what the executive branch told the judicial branch.”

Attorney Brad Moss, who specializes in cases pertaining to national security and federal employment law, contended that while “time will tell” what information was provided to the courts in advance, “this entire situation reeks of political vendetta.”

Asserting that Omar’s path to U.S. citizenship had long “been the subject of conservative fever dreams,” Moss said there was also a bigger picture to consider.

“To do this mere weeks before the midterms, in defiance of all measure of established rules and guidelines, is just further proof of the ‘go ahead and stop me’ mentality of the Trump White House,” he said.

Whatever else happens, it seems unlikely that the raid will seriously imperil Omar’s chances of reelection.

Last time out, in 2024, she won her heavily Democratic district by roughly 50 points.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Trump says he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle
articles.summary: "Well, we're looking at it," President Trump said when asked if he's considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.
articles.body:
Washington — President Trump said he and his administration are "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle from her position as U.S. ambassador to Greece, after an associate of Guilfoyle's alleged she asked him to wire $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing.

"Well, we're looking at it," the president told reporters on his way to Ohio when asked if he's considering firing Guilfoyle. "We're not happy."

Guilfoyle is aware that Mr. Trump is debating firing her, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. She has been talking to her lawyer and asking Trump administration aides for advice, the sources said.

Businessman Eric Deters told CBS News last week he has "no doubt it was pay-to-play" when Guilfoyle asked for funds. Deters also provided CBS News with screenshots of his texts with Guilfoyle, including one message in which she appeared to ask him to wire money. Deters said he never gave her the money.

"Unfortunately for Kimberly Guilfoyle, at that time, at that moment in time, I didn't have $100,000 to spare to give to Kimberly Guilfoyle, or I actually would have been a dumbass enough to do it."

White House officials were told that the text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters were authentic, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News last week. Some Trump aides expressed displeasure about Guilfoyle's actions, they said.

Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of the texts to The Wall Street Journal, which was first to report on them.

The Journal also reported this weekend that Guilfoyle boasted in audio recordings about Greek businessmen who paid for her travel, and reportedly encouraged foreign governments to do business with one of the tycoons.

Guilfoyle, nominated by Mr. Trump to serve as his top envoy to Greece, is the ex-fiancée of Donald Trump Jr. Her confirmation hearing was held in July 2025, and she was confirmed in September of that year.

She was highly visible during Secretary of State Marco Rubio's visit to Greece last week. At the time, Rubio did not respond to questions about Deter's allegations, telling reporters: "I'm not going to comment on a story that literally posted a few hours ago."
